title: Poetry and Sound
objectives: I can explain what ten words about poems and songs mean.
I can find rhyme, rhythm, and verses in a poem and tell what makes it sound like music.
I can use poetry words to talk about how a poem sounds and what it makes me imagine.
I can write and share a short poem using words from this unit.
rationale: Fourth graders read, recite, and write poems, but they often lack the words to talk about how a poem works. This unit gives them three Tier 3 forms (rhyme, verse, haiku) and seven Tier 2 words for performance and craft (chorus, melody, recite, compose, rhythm, poetic, applaud). The sequence moves from the building blocks of a poem (rhyme, rhythm, verse) to song parts (chorus, melody), to what poets and students do (compose, recite) and how an audience responds (applaud). It follows the narrative unit with poetry and revisits audition from the sound unit through a performance setting.

passage.title: Poems Make Music with Words
paras: A poem is a piece of writing that uses words the way a song uses sound. Poets choose each word carefully, and they often play with how the words sound. One common tool is rhyme, when two words end with the same sound, like moon and spoon. Another is rhythm, the pattern of strong and soft beats in the words.

Many poems are made of groups of lines called verses. A song may have verses too, along with a chorus, a part that repeats after each verse so listeners can sing along. A melody is the tune that goes with the words. Songwriters compose both the words and the tune.

Some poems are very short. A haiku is a short poem, often with three lines of five, seven, and five syllables. Many haiku are about nature. Here is one: "Soft rain on the roof / Puddles gather by the door / Frogs begin to sing." The words are poetic, painting a picture with only a few details.

Poems are meant to be heard. A student may recite a poem from memory, speaking slowly so the rhythm and rhymes are clear. When the performance is over, the audience will applaud, clapping to show they enjoyed it.

qs.why: Each paragraph shows how poems work: sounds, verses and song parts, short forms, and performance.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words about poems and songs and then use them to talk about how a poem sounds. They find rhymes and rhythms, mark verses and choruses, and write and perform a short poem.

notes.va.rhyme.n: Rhymes depend on sound, not spelling: blue and shoe rhyme but look different. Have students listen first, then spell. A common error is thinking words that start alike rhyme.
notes.va.verse.n: Verse means a group of lines in this unit; mention that it also names poetry in general. Use a song the class knows to count verses.
notes.va.haiku.n: In English classrooms, the five-seven-five pattern is common but Japanese haiku count sound units differently. Accept short three-line poems about nature and avoid treating the count as a strict rule.
notes.va.chorus.n: Contrast with verse: the chorus repeats, the verses change. The group-of-singers sense appears in school chorus. Ask students which sense a sentence uses.
notes.va.melody.n: Hum it. Melody is the tune; rhythm is the beat. Play a short tune and a drum pattern separately to show the difference.
notes.va.recite.v: Recite means to say aloud, often from memory. Re- + cite. Plan a gentle recitation with a short poem; give students choices so no one is forced to perform alone.
notes.va.compose.v: Compose is creating something new, in music or writing. Students sometimes confuse compose with copy. Show a blank page and a pencil.
notes.va.rhythm.n: Spelling is tricky; teach it as a word to learn by sight. Clap syllables in names to feel the beat.
notes.va.poetic.adj: Poet + -ic. A poetic description uses images and feeling. Ask students to make a plain sentence poetic.
notes.va.applaud.v: Applaud has two uses: clapping and showing approval in words. Practice audience manners and respectful applause for each performer.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The song has a part that repeats after each verse. That repeating part is the chorus. I can hum the melody, the tune, and clap the rhythm, the beat. Now I can tell the parts apart with the right words.'
